name: ACP-105
lead: ACP-105 is an investigational nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) with partial agonist activity relative to testosterone, described in a 2009 Journal of Medicinal Chemistry paper [1][2]. It was discovered through a high-throughput screen using receptor selection and amplification technology, and improved anabolic parameters in castrated male rats [1].

Later animal work examined it in models of cognitive decline and radiation-related deficits [3][4]. It is not approved; SARMs are banned in sport, and metabolism studies in humans-targeted and equine doping control have been published [5][6].

paras: In a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, ACP-105 alone and with an estrogen receptor beta agonist was reported to moderate cognitive deficits and amyloid-beta levels [3]. A 2011 study examined its effects on rotarod performance and fear conditioning in sham-irradiated and irradiated female mice [4].
No studies found in humans. All published efficacy work is in cells and animals [1][3][4].

No human safety data were identified for ACP-105. Reviews of the class describe elevated liver enzymes, reduced HDL cholesterol and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in some trials, case reports linking recreational SARM use to liver injury, and unknown cardiovascular risk; the US FDA states that SARMs are unapproved and cannot legally be marketed as supplements or drugs. [7]
Doping-control papers have characterised its mass spectrometric behaviour and metabolites, including in horses [5][6].

card.summary: A discontinued experimental SARM tested in rats and mice; no human trials, sold online as a research chemical.
card.note: Preclinical only; banned in sport; no human safety data.

quick.overview:
ACP-105 is an experimental SARM from the late 2000s. Rodent studies showed muscle-related effects and some cognitive findings.

No human trials were found; it is unapproved.
quick.mechanism: It acts as a partial agonist at the androgen receptor, producing smaller effects than testosterone in tissues tested in rats.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown. SARMs as a class are banned in sport and have been linked in reports to liver injury and hormone suppression.
